passage:
Gurleen had opened her acceptance mail at nineteen and felt no joy at all, only a flicker of dread. At the institute, her batch-mates talked about summer research and famous mentors. She told her friend Abhinav, "They'll realise soon that they picked the wrong file." When he said her project was the best in the lab, she answered, "The topic was easy." Every night she compared her notes with theirs and saw only the gaps.
At twenty-four, she began at a logistics firm. In Monday meetings, colleagues spoke with easy certainty, and Gurleen sat with a pen and an unread list of thoughts. Inside she was full of questions. Outside, everyone else looked sure. She said nothing week after week. When a new client project was assigned, the manager gave it to Joseph, who had spoken up about a route problem that Gurleen had also noticed. Gurleen looked at her notebook. "See? Nobody thinks I add much," she thought. She did not notice that nobody had heard what she thought in the first place.

qa.q: Who did the manager give the new client project to?
qa.a: The manager gave it to Joseph, who had spoken up about a route problem.

qa.q: How does Gurleen's habit at the logistics firm connect to how she felt at the institute?
qa.a: At the institute she compared her notes with theirs and saw only the gaps. At the firm she compared her inside questions with everyone else's sure manner and stayed silent, and the silence made her less visible, which fed her belief that she added little.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she said nothing in Monday meetings?
qa.a: She felt insecure and doubtful, thinking everyone else was sure while she was only full of questions.

qa.q: What could Gurleen do to make herself heard in meetings?
qa.a: She can share one point from her list each week, and ask Joseph or a trusted colleague how they decide when to speak.

grounding: Fraud feelings and harsh comparison at a top college (4092) become silence in meetings at a new job that makes the person less visible (3230): one person over years.
